summary.text: Assuming density \(1/2\), upper and lower bounds on the even counts, together with growth of the monovariant \(a_k+2a_{k+1}\) at every step not joining two even terms, force suitable earlier terms to be exponentially large. Any sufficiently late adjacent difference of \(1\) then makes transformed first differences double backward, forcing a linearly long block of even terms whose count contradicts the density bounds.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
H(x)=\begin{cases}x/2,&x\text{ even},\\x,&x\text{ odd}.
\end{cases}
\]
The sequence in question is
\[
a_0=1,
\qquad a_1=3,
\qquad a_{n+2}=H(a_{n+1})+H(a_n).
\]
We prove that the following two assertions cannot both hold:

1. the set of indices \(n\) for which \(a_n\) is even has natural density \(1/2\);
2. there are infinitely many \(n\) for which \(|a_{n+1}-a_n|=1\).

Thus their conjunction, which is the stated conjecture, is false.

Throughout, all sequence terms are positive. Indeed, \(a_0,a_1>0\), and \(H(x)\ge 1\) whenever \(x\ge1\), so the recurrence preserves positivity. We shall repeatedly use the elementary inequalities
\[
H(x)\le x\le 2H(x).
\tag{1}
\]

## 1. Two elementary bounds between consecutive terms

We first record
\[
a_n\le 2a_{n+1}
\tag{2}
\]
and
\[
a_{n+1}\le 3a_n
\tag{3}
\]
for every \(n\ge0\).

For (2), the case \(n=0\) is immediate. If \(n=m+1\), then
\[
a_{m+2}=H(a_{m+1})+H(a_m)\ge H(a_{m+1})\ge \frac{a_{m+1}}2,
\]
by (1), which gives \(a_{m+1}\le2a_{m+2}\).

For (3), again the initial case is immediate. For \(n=m+1\), using (1) and then (2),
\[
a_{m+2}=H(a_{m+1})+H(a_m)
 \le a_{m+1}+a_m
 \le a_{m+1}+2a_{m+1}=3a_{m+1}.
\]

## 2. A growth estimate

Define
\[
P_k=a_k+2a_{k+1}.
\]
Also let \(N(k)\) be the number of indices \(r\in\{0,1,\ldots,k-1\}\) for which \(a_r\) and \(a_{r+1}\) are not both even. We call such an \(r\) a non-even-even step.

First, \(P_k\) is nondecreasing. Put \(x=a_k\), \(y=a_{k+1}\), \(u=H(x)\), and \(v=H(y)\). Then \(a_{k+2}=u+v\), and hence
\[
P_{k+1}=y+2u+2v.
\]
Since \(x\le2u\) and \(y\le2v\),
\[
P_k=x+2y\le2u+y+2v=P_{k+1}.
\tag{4}
\]

At a non-even-even step we have the stronger estimate
\[
15P_k\le14P_{k+1}.
\tag{5}
\]
There are two substantive parity cases.

If \(y=a_{k+1}\) is odd, then \(v=y\), so
\[
P_{k+1}=3y+2u.
\]
Thus (5) is equivalent to
\[
15x+30y\le28u+42y,
\]
or \(15x\le28u+12y\). This follows from \(x\le2u\), which gives \(14x\le28u\), and \(x\le2y\), which certainly gives \(x\le12y\).

If \(y\) is even, then the step being non-even-even forces \(x\) to be odd. Hence \(v=y/2\) and \(u=x\), so
\[
P_{k+1}=2x+2y.
\]
Now (5) reduces to
\[
15x+30y\le28x+28y,
\]
i.e. \(2y\le13x\), which follows from the previously proved bound \(y\le3x\).

Since \(P_0=1+2\cdot3=7\), iterating (4) at even-even steps and (5) at non-even-even steps gives
\[
15^{N(k)}\,7\le14^{N(k)}P_k.
\tag{6}
\]
By (3),
\[
P_k=a_k+2a_{k+1}\le a_k+6a_k=7a_k.
\]
After substituting this into (6) and cancelling \(7\), we obtain
\[
15^{N(k)}\le14^{N(k)}a_k.
\tag{7}
\]

We will use the following consequence:
\[
14m\le N(k)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad a_k\ge2^m.
\tag{8}
\]
Indeed, if \(N=N(k)\ge14m\), write \(N=14m+r\). Since
\[
2\cdot14^{14}\le15^{14},
\]
raising this inequality to the \(m\)-th power and using \(14^r\le15^r\) gives
\[
2^m14^N\le15^N.
\]
Combining this with (7) yields
\[
2^m14^N\le a_k14^N,
\]
and cancellation of the positive number \(14^N\) proves (8).

## 3. The difference dynamics

Define
\[
g_k=H(a_k).
\]
The recurrence for \(a\) gives
\[
a_{k+2}=g_{k+1}+g_k,
\]
and therefore
\[
g_{k+2}=H(g_{k+1}+g_k).
\tag{9}
\]
Define the integer-valued differences
\[
e_k=g_{k+1}-g_k.
\]
The integers \(g_{k+1}-g_k\) and \(g_{k+1}+g_k\) have the same parity. Consequently,
\[
e_k\text{ is even}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 g_{k+1}+g_k\text{ is even}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad a_{k+2}\text{ is even}.
\tag{10}
\]

Equation (9) gives two simple transition rules for \(e_k\).

If \(e_k\) is even, then \(g_{k+1}+g_k\) is even, and hence
\[
g_{k+2}=\frac{g_{k+1}+g_k}{2}.
\]
It follows that
\[
2e_{k+1}=2(g_{k+2}-g_{k+1})=g_k-g_{k+1}=-e_k.
\tag{11}
\]

If \(e_k\) is odd, then \(g_{k+1}+g_k\) is odd and is not halved, so
\[
g_{k+2}=g_{k+1}+g_k,
\qquad e_{k+1}=g_k.
\tag{12}
\]

These rules imply a useful backward-doubling principle. If
\[
a_k>2|e_{k+1}|,
\tag{13}
\]
then
\[
e_k=-2e_{k+1}.
\tag{14}
\]
For if \(e_k\) is even, this is exactly (11). If \(e_k\) is odd, (12) says \(|e_{k+1}|=g_k=H(a_k)\). But (1) gives \(a_k\le2H(a_k)=2|e_{k+1}|\), contradicting (13). Thus the odd case is impossible.

We also need to translate a difference-one event for the original sequence into an initial value for this backward process. Directly from \(a_{m+3}=g_{m+2}+g_{m+1}\) and \(a_{m+2}=g_{m+1}+g_m\),
\[
a_{m+3}-a_{m+2}=e_{m+1}+e_m.
\tag{15}
\]
Suppose
\[
|a_{m+3}-a_{m+2}|=1
\quad\text{and}\quad a_{m+1}>2.
\tag{16}
\]
Then
\[
|e_m|=2.
\tag{17}
\]
To prove this, first suppose \(e_m\) is even. By (11), \(e_m=-2e_{m+1}\), so
\[
e_{m+1}+e_m=-e_{m+1}.
\]
Equations (15) and (16) therefore give \(|e_{m+1}|=1\), and hence \(|e_m|=2\).

If instead \(e_m\) is odd, then (12) gives \(e_{m+1}=g_m\). Thus
\[
e_{m+1}+e_m=g_m+(g_{m+1}-g_m)=g_{m+1}.
\]
Its absolute value being \(1\) forces \(g_{m+1}=H(a_{m+1})=1\). The definition of \(H\) then implies \(a_{m+1}\le2\), contrary to (16). This eliminates the odd case and proves (17).

Iterating the backward-doubling principle yields the following chain statement. If
\[
|e_{b+i}|=2
\tag{18}
\]
and
\[
a_{b+i-j}>2^{j+1}\qquad(1\le j\le i),
\tag{19}
\]
then
\[
|e_b|=2^{i+1}.
\tag{20}
\]
This follows by induction on \(i\). For \(i=0\), it is just (18). In the inductive step, first apply the assertion to the chain ending at \(b+i+1\) but beginning at \(b+1\), obtaining
\[
|e_{b+1}|=2^{i+1}.
\]
The last instance of (19), namely \(a_b>2^{i+2}=2|e_{b+1}|\), then permits (14) at \(b\), giving
\[
|e_b|=2|e_{b+1}|=2^{i+2}.
\]

## 4. Consequences of density \(1/2\)

Assume, for contradiction, that both parts of the conjecture hold.

Let
\[
E(b)=\#\{0\le r<b:a_r\text{ is even}\}.
\]
The density assumption says
\[
\frac{E(b)}b\longrightarrow\frac12.
\]
Therefore there are thresholds \(K_U,K_L\) such that for every \(b\ge K_U\),
\[
200E(b)\le101b,
\tag{21}
\]
and for every \(b\ge K_L\),
\[
99b\le200E(b).
\tag{22}
\]
These are simply eventual bounds placing the ratio \(E(b)/b\) between \(99/200\) and \(101/200\).

The two counts \(E(b)\) and \(N(b)\) satisfy
\[
b\le E(b)+N(b).
\tag{23}
\]
Indeed, for each \(r<b\), either \(a_r\) is even, in which case \(r\) is counted by \(E(b)\), or \(a_r\) is odd, in which case \(a_r,a_{r+1}\) cannot both be even, so \(r\) is counted by \(N(b)\). Some indices may be counted by both, which is why (23) is an inequality.

Combining (21) and (23), for every \(b\ge K_U\) we get
\[
200b\le200N(b)+200E(b)\le200N(b)+101b,

after which
\[
99b\le200N(b).
\tag{24}
\]

A useful consequence is the following. If
\[
36j+72\le n,
\qquad K_U\le n-2-j,
\tag{25}
\]
then
\[
a_{n-2-j}>2^{j+1}.
\tag{26}
\]
Put \(b=n-2-j\). By (24),
\[
99(n-2-j)\le200N(n-2-j).
\]
The first inequality in (25) implies, by straightforward arithmetic,
\[
200\cdot14(j+2)\le99(n-2-j).
\]
Hence \(14(j+2)\le N(n-2-j)\). Applying (8) with \(m=j+2\) gives
\[
a_{n-2-j}\ge2^{j+2}>2^{j+1},
\]
which is (26).

## 5. A late difference-one event forces a long even block

Because the difference-one indices are assumed infinite, they are unbounded. Choose such an index \(n\) so large that
\[
n>40K_U+40K_L+100000.
\tag{27}
\]
Thus
\[
|a_{n+1}-a_n|=1.
\tag{28}
\]
Set
\[
L=\left\lfloor\frac{n-72}{36}\right\rfloor.
\tag{29}
\]
The generous lower bound (27) ensures all indices used below exceed the required density thresholds.

We first show that \(a_{n-1}>2\). Since \(n-1\ge K_U\), (24) gives
\[
99(n-1)\le200N(n-1).
\]
As \(n\) is much larger than \(100000\), this implies \(N(n-1)\ge28=14\cdot2\). By (8),
\[
a_{n-1}\ge2^2=4>2.
\tag{30}
\]

Apply (15) with \(m=n-2\). Equation (28) says
\[
|e_{n-1}+e_{n-2}|=1,
\]
and (30) supplies the required inequality \(a_{n-1}>2\). The conclusion (17) is therefore
\[
|e_{n-2}|=2.
\tag{31}
\]

For every \(j\) with \(1\le j\le L\), the definition of \(L\) gives
\[
36j+72\le n.
\]
Moreover, (27) ensures \(n-2-j\ge K_U\). Thus (26) gives
\[
a_{n-2-j}>2^{j+1}\qquad(1\le j\le L).
\tag{32}
\]

Fix any \(t\) with \(0\le t\le L\). Apply the backward chain (18)–(20) with
\[
b=n-2-t,
\qquad i=t.
\]
Its endpoint condition is (31), and all its size conditions are supplied by (32). We obtain
\[
|e_{n-2-t}|=2^{t+1}.
\tag{33}
\]
In particular, \(e_{n-2-t}\) is even. By the parity equivalence (10),
\[
a_{n-t}\text{ is even}.
\tag{34}
\]
Since this holds for every \(0\le t\le L\), every term in the entire interval
\[
a_{n-L},a_{n-L+1},\ldots,a_n
\]
is even. This is a block of \(L+1\) consecutive even terms.

## 6. The long even block contradicts density \(1/2\)

The even block gives the exact counting identity
\[
E(n+1)=E(n-L)+(L+1).
\tag{35}
\]
The choice (27) and the bound \(L\le(n-72)/36\) imply \(n-L\ge K_L\), while plainly \(n+1\ge K_U\). We may therefore apply the lower density estimate (22) at \(n-L\) and the upper density estimate (21) at \(n+1\):
\[
99(n-L)\le200E(n-L)
\tag{36}
\]
and
\[
200E(n+1)\le101(n+1).
\tag{37}
\]
Using (35) between (36) and (37),
\[
99(n-L)+200(L+1)
 \le200E(n-L)+200(L+1)
 =200E(n+1)
 \le101(n+1).
\]
After simplification, this is
\[
101L+99\le2n.
\tag{38}
\]

On the other hand, from the definition (29) of the floor, the remainder on division of \(n-72\) by \(36\) is at most \(35\), so
\[
n\le36L+107.
\tag{39}
\]
Combining (38) and twice (39) gives
\[
101L+99\le2n\le72L+214.
\]
Therefore
\[
29L\le115,
\]
so \(L\le3\). Equation (39) then gives \(n\le215\), contradicting the choice \(n>100000\) in (27).

This contradiction arose solely from assuming simultaneously that the even terms have natural density \(1/2\) and that infinitely many adjacent pairs differ by \(1\). Hence those two claims cannot both be true. Therefore the conjectured conjunction for OEIS A120424 is false.
